EAQ108.brief: PCG stands for Procedural Content Generation. It is a system in Unreal where a graph of nodes places objects for you by rules, so you do not place each one by hand. PCG Mode adds tools on top of this that let you draw a spline or paint an area in the level, and a PCG graph then fills it with props. In this quest you build a graph that places props along a spline, make it usable as a tool, and make a second one that you paint with.
checklist: Enable the Procedural Content Generation Framework plugin. Then create a PCG Graph named PCG_FenceProps.

In PCG_FenceProps, connect these nodes in a row: Get Spline Data, then Spline Sampler, then Transform Points with a small random yaw and scale, then Static Mesh Spawner. Give the spawner three Mesh Entries (a post, a barrel and a crate) with different Weights, so some appear more often than others.
Open the Graph Settings. Under Tool Data, set Display Name to Fence Props, add SplineTool to Compatible Tool Tags, and enable Is Preset.
Switch to PCG mode from the Modes dropdown. With nothing selected, choose the Draw Spline tool and pick your Fence Props preset. Draw an open spline along a path in your level and click Apply.

Duplicate the graph and name the copy PCG_Rubble. Remove the spline nodes, keep the spawner, and set Compatible Tool Tags to PaintTool. In PCG mode, use the Paint tool to paint rubble on the ground. Hold Shift to remove points that land on the path.
In the Raycast Rules, enable Ignore PCG Components. This stops you from painting on top of the props you already spawned.
EAQ108.done_when: Send one screenshot of the level that shows the props placed along the spline and the painted rubble. Also send one screenshot of PCG_FenceProps with its Tool Data settings visible.

EAQ109.brief: The Procedural Foliage tool grows a forest for you by simulating how plants spread. Each type of tree has rules, such as how much shade it makes and whether it can grow in the shade of others, so the types compete for space the way real plants do. In this quest you set up a spawner with a big tree and a small tree, adjust their rules, and use a blocking volume to keep an area free of trees.
checklist: Open Editor Preferences, then Experimental, and enable Procedural Foliage. Create a Procedural Foliage Spawner named PFS_Forest and scale it over a flat area of a landscape.
Create two Static Mesh Foliage assets named SMF_TreeBig and SMF_TreeSmall. Add both to the Foliage Types of PFS_Forest and press Resimulate.

In SMF_TreeBig, set Shade Radius to 50 and Overlap Priority to 2. In SMF_TreeSmall, set Overlap Priority to 1 and enable Can Grow in Shade and Spawns in Shade. Press Resimulate and look at how the small trees fill the space around the big ones.
Change Num Steps to 0 on SMF_TreeBig and press Resimulate. Then set it back to 3. Lower Initial Seed Density until the edge of the forest looks natural.
In the Instance Settings of both types, set Cull Distance Max to 20000.
Place a Procedural Foliage Blocking Volume over your path or over the place where a building stands, and press Resimulate. No trees should appear inside the volume.
EAQ109.done_when: Send two screenshots, one of the forest before the blocking volume and one after it. Also send one screenshot of the Procedural settings of SMF_TreeSmall (Collision, Clustering and Growth).

EAQ110.brief: Geometry Script is a plugin that lets a Blueprint create and change meshes with nodes. With it you can build your own small tools, for example one that scatters rocks, and change how they work without help from a programmer. In this quest you build a Blueprint that scatters simple shapes inside a circle, with variables for how many, how far and which random pattern.
checklist: Open Edit > Plugins, search for geometry script, and enable the Geometry Script plugin. Restart the editor.

Create a Blueprint with the parent class GeneratedDynamicMeshActor and name it BP_GS_RockScatter. Add three public variables: Count (Integer, default 30), Radius (Float, default 800) and Seed (Integer). Make all three Instance Editable, so you can change them in the Details panel.
In the Event Graph, add the event named Event On Rebuild Generated Mesh. Promote its Target Mesh pin to a variable named DynamicMesh.

Make a Random Stream from Seed and add a loop that runs Count times. In each step of the loop, build a Transform with a random position inside Radius, a random yaw and a random scale. Then use Append Box (or Append Sphere) to add a shape to DynamicMesh at that transform.
Place BP_GS_RockScatter in your level. Change Count, Radius and Seed in the Details panel and watch the scatter rebuild.
Write two lines in your notes: why the same Target Mesh pin goes in and out of every node, and why you should not use this actor for 5000 instanced rocks.
EAQ110.done_when: Send one screenshot of the level with the scattered rocks and one screenshot of the Event Graph. Add your two lines of notes to the message.

EAQ111.brief: The Pattern tool in Modeling Mode makes many copies of a mesh in a line, a grid or a circle. It is a quick way to build fences, tiled floors and rings of columns. The copies can be created as instances, which means Unreal draws them together as one group and saves performance. In this quest you make all three patterns and then edit and convert the instances.
checklist: Open Modeling Mode with Shift+5. Select one fence post mesh and open XForm, then Pattern. Use the Line shape to make a row of 12 posts. Set the output type to Instanced Static Mesh and accept.
Select a floor tile and use Pattern with the Grid shape to make a floor of 6x6 tiles. Add a small rotation jitter, a little random rotation, so the tiles do not all look the same.
Select a torch or column mesh and use Pattern with the Circle shape to place 8 copies around a center. This time, output them as single actors.
Select the 8 single actors and run XForm, then Harvest Instances. This turns them into one ISM actor, which is one actor that holds all the instances.
Open XForm, then ISMEd, on the fence row. Delete two instances and move one. Then replace one instance with a different mesh and look at the list of components.
Compare the Outliner before and after. Count the actors in the fence row and in the circle after you harvested it.
EAQ111.done_when: Send one screenshot of the level with the three patterns (line, grid and circle). Also send one screenshot of the Details panel of the fence ISM actor that shows its instanced components.

EAQ112.brief: In a large world that uses World Partition, Unreal only loads the parts of the level near the player. Far parts are unloaded, so distant buildings and trees would simply disappear. HLOD, which means Hierarchical Level of Detail, replaces those far parts with cheap stand-in meshes that stay visible. An HLOD Layer is an asset that decides how the stand-in is made. In this quest you create two HLOD Layers, assign them to buildings and trees, and build the HLODs.
checklist: In a World Partition level, open the Content Drawer and create two HLOD Layer assets (choose Miscellaneous, then HLOD Layer). Name one HLOD_Buildings and set its Layer Type to Merged Mesh. Name the other HLOD_Trees and set its Layer Type to Instancing.
On HLOD_Buildings, enable Generate Nanite Enabled Mesh and turn Merge Materials on. On HLOD_Trees, leave the Instancing settings at their defaults.
Select your building meshes and set their Mobility to Static. In the Details panel, set the HLOD property to HLOD_Buildings. Do the same for the tree actors, with HLOD_Trees.
In World Settings, set Default HLOD Layer to HLOD_Buildings, so that new static actors get a layer by default.
Run Build > Build HLODs. Then move the camera far away, or unload cells, and compare the view with HLODs on and off.
Open one of the generated HLOD actors and note its Cell Size and Loading Range. Write one line on why the trees used Instancing and the buildings used Merged Mesh.
EAQ112.done_when: Send two screenshots from the same far camera position, one with the HLODs showing and one without. Also send a screenshot of the settings of the two HLOD Layer assets.

EAQ113.brief: When you place the same mesh many times, Unreal can draw all copies together as instances and avoid one draw call, one drawing job, for each copy. The Instanced Static Mesh component (ISM) and the Hierarchical Instanced Static Mesh component (HISM) both do this. In this quest you measure the draw calls of 100 separate props, batch them into instances, and build a shelf Blueprint with each of the two component types.
checklist: Place 100 copies of one book mesh or brick mesh as separate Static Mesh Actors. In the console, type stat unit and stat rhi, and note the number of draw calls.
Select all 100 actors. Open Actor, then Merge Actors, then Merge Actors Settings. Choose the Batch method and click Merge Actors. Note the draw calls again.
Open the Details panel of the new actor. Click one instance and confirm that you can only edit its transform. Then change the material on the component and see all instances update.
Create a Blueprint named BP_Shelf with an Instanced Static Mesh component. Set its Static Mesh, and add 10 instances with the + button in the Instances category.

Duplicate BP_Shelf and name the copy BP_Shelf_HISM. Use a Hierarchical Instanced Static Mesh component in it. Write two lines: which component you would use for 5000 static pebbles, and which one for a project that uses only Nanite.

On the ISM, enable Per Instance Custom Data by setting Num Custom Data Floats to 1. Use this value in the material to control the color, so that two shelves can look different without a new material instance.
EAQ113.done_when: Send a screenshot of the stat numbers before batching and after batching, and a screenshot of the components of BP_Shelf. Add your two lines of notes.

EAQ114.brief: A Data Layer is a named group of actors in a World Partition level that you can load and unload together. This lets one level hold several versions of its decoration, for example a winter look and a summer look, without copying the whole map. In this quest you create three Data Layers, decorate one area in two ways, and switch between the two versions while the game runs.
checklist: In a World Partition level, open the Content Browser and create three Data Layer assets (choose Miscellaneous, then Data Layer). Name them DL_Dressing_Base with the Editor type, DL_Dressing_Winter with the Runtime type, and DL_Dressing_Summer with the Runtime type.
Open Window > World Partition > Data Layer Outliner. Drag each asset into it to create a Data Layer Instance.

Right-click DL_Dressing_Base in the outliner and choose Make Current Data Layer. Place your permanent props and confirm that they are assigned to the layer automatically. Then choose Clear Current Data Layers.

Decorate one area twice. Assign snow piles and bare trees to DL_Dressing_Winter, and assign flowers and leafy trees to DL_Dressing_Summer. Use Add Selected Actors to Selected Data Layer to assign them.
Set Initial Runtime State so that Summer is Activated and Winter is Unloaded. Use the visibility checkbox and the Loaded In Editor checkbox to look at each version.
In the Level Blueprint, add a key press event. Use the Data Layer Subsystem to set Winter to Activated and Summer to Unloaded. Test it while playing in the editor.
EAQ114.done_when: Send two screenshots of the same area, one in its Winter version and one in its Summer version. Also send a screenshot of the Data Layer Outliner that shows all three layers and their types.

EAQ115.brief: When other people review your art, they need pictures that show the same view before and after a change, at a size where small details are visible. Unreal has a High Resolution Screenshot tool for this, and bookmarks that bring the camera back to exactly the same view. In this quest you save three bookmarks and use the tool to take large captures, a capture of one region, images without lighting, and a cutout of one prop.
checklist: Set three world bookmarks (1, 2 and 3) on views of your decorated area. Bookmarks let you return to the same view, so every capture can be repeated.
Open Viewport Options, then High Resolution Screenshot. Set the Screenshot Size Multiplier to 2 and capture bookmark 1. Find the file in the folder Saved/Screenshots/Windows.
Press Specify Region and drag a region around one group of props. Capture again, and then clear the region.
Enable Include Buffer Visualization Targets and capture bookmark 2. Open the BaseColor image and the Roughness image, and check that your props are still easy to read without lighting.
Select one main prop and enable Render CustomDepth Pass in its Details panel. In the screenshot tool, enable Use custom depth as mask, and capture a cutout of the prop.
Play in the editor, open the console and run HighResShot 2 for bookmark 3. Name the files Review_<area>_<bookmark> and post them together.
EAQ115.done_when: Send three review captures of the same bookmarks, the BaseColor buffer image, and the custom depth cutout. All files must be named as the checklist says.
